title: Your own breath
hook: thousands of breaths a day, nearly all of them unnoticed: notice ten

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vast silence, and your line was let all the earth keep silence. Today, the one sound that never left.

You've been breathing this whole lesson. In, out, in, on its own. It will keep going while you scroll, argue, cook and forget. How many in a day? Some people guess around twenty thousand. No one counts their own, and the real number shifts with sleep and stairs and worry. But even as a guess, it's a crowd, slipping by one after another, unnoticed. After trees, storms, paintings and silence, today awe is right under your nose.
screen: `IN, OUT, ON ITS OWN.` → `A GUESS: TWENTY THOUSAND.` → `AWE UNDER YOUR NOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the breath given. In the second chapter of Genesis, God shapes the first human from the dust of the ground and, in the King James wording, "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Before the breath, a shape of dust. After it, someone alive. The story puts breath at the border between dust and life. Second, the breath remembered. In the Book of Job, a young man named Elihu speaks up: "The spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life." For Elihu, every breath is a reminder of where life came from. Third, the breath watched. In the Buddhist teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, the Buddha describes a practitioner who sits down and simply knows the breath: breathing in a long breath, knowing it's long; breathing in a short breath, knowing it's short. No changing it, no judging it. That simple attention is where the practice begins. Fourth, why it's awe. Awe tends to get saved for the rare and the far: the night sky, the ocean. But the breath is constant and near, and it isn't yours to command. You can hold it a while, but you can't stop it for good, and you don't have to start it each time. Some paths name a giver behind it, as Genesis and Job do. Others simply watch it, as the Buddha's teaching does.
screen: `GENESIS: THE BREATH OF LIFE.` · `JOB: THE BREATH OF THE ALMIGHTY.` · `THE BUDDHA: KNOWING THE BREATH.` · `CONSTANT, NEAR, NOT YOURS TO COMMAND.` · then, large: `A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Let your breath do whatever it's already doing, and notice ten breaths, one at a time: where the air comes in, the nose, the throat, the chest or belly, and where it goes out. When you lose count, begin again at one; that's part of the practice, not a failure. If you pray, let each breath be a quiet thank you; if you don't, simply know each breath as it comes.
Elihu. The young man in Job who said, the breath of the Almighty hath given me life, alongside the breath of life in Genesis and the breath simply known in the Buddha's teaching. Today's word.
Your line: twenty thousand. A crowd of breaths, and each one arrives on its own. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Attention to the breath is a meditation practice in Buddhist teaching on mindfulness, and the breath appears in Genesis and Job as the gift of life; some people count ten breaths as a short daily practice.

chat.says: What's so amazing about breathing? I do it all day without thinking.
options: It's constant and near, yet not yours to command; you can't stop it for good.
Breathing is amazing only for athletes and singers, who train their lungs.
It's just a reflex; awe is for rare and faraway things, like the night sky.
